note: THE MECHANIC. A rumpled old man in a brown tweed suit: wild white
hair, round glasses, a white moustache, an open jacket over a
waistcoat and a shirt, a dark red bow tie, brown trousers and heavy
brown shoes. Painted off the reference sheet.
Every number is a fraction of the figure: yN is height with 0 at the
sole and 1 at the crown, ax is |x| over the fingertip reach, all read
in the T-pose the rig is bound in.
THE BANDS ARE MEASURED, NOT PLACED. What the rig said, per bone:
shoulder ax 0.149-0.222 arm ax 0.161-0.554
forearm  ax 0.532-0.719 hand ax 0.733-0.858
So the chin is at 0.751 and the cuff is at 0.73, and both of those are
the mesh's own numbers rather than a guess off the drawing.
A THIRD OF THE MESH IS HEAD — 37,686 vertices of the 81,084 — and
nearly all of that is hair. It is the one thing about this character
the whole mass of it rather than just the crown.
THE JACKET IS OPEN, which the painter could not say until now. `panel`
is the OUTSIDE of the torso and a waistcoat is the inside, so `front`
is a new strip that takes depth into account — see classify() in
paint-skinned.js. Without the z test the waistcoat appears down his
spine as well.
NOT PAINTED: the glasses and the moustache. Both are geometry sitting
on the face at a scale no height band can find, and a band wide enough
to catch the glasses takes the eyes with it. At the distance this
character is ever seen from — standing in a workshop, several metres
off — the white hair and the brown suit are the whole read.
NO hatLine. It is the first thing the head branch tests and it returns
before the face is considered — which is exactly right for a hat, whose
whole point is covering the fringe, and exactly wrong for hair. Painting
this head with one gave him a white face. `hair` is the colour and the
face is the window in it, which is what the head branch already does.
NOT PAINTED: the moustache. It is modelled, it sits inside the face
ellipse, and bands do not reach the head — so it comes out skin. At the
distance he is seen from it reads as a face, and the alternative is a
white bar across the whole head at that height.
